title: Byte Pair Encoding for Efficient Time Series Forecasting
one_liner: Instead of chopping time series into fixed-size chunks, group repeating patterns into tokens and compress adaptively.
lead: Time series forecasting models currently chop sequences into equal-sized pieces, then turn each piece into a token (a single number used by the model). But this wastes tokens on simple parts like flat stretches, and requires expensive computation. This paper proposes pattern-based tokenization: find the most common short patterns (motifs) in your data, then merge all matching stretches into single tokens, compressing the sequence intelligently.

problem.h2: Fixed-size chunks waste tokens on simple patterns
paras: Today's time series models convert sequences into tokens (compressed units the model processes). The standard approach: divide a time series into equal-sized blocks regardless of what is happening in the data. A flat price over 100 days becomes 100 tokens. An identical pattern repeated five times becomes five tokens per repetition, ten tokens wasted.

Why does this break? Models have a limited attention window (the maximum length they can process per step). More tokens means you hit that limit faster, forcing expensive operations: breaking long sequences into pieces, discarding data, or running the model multiple times on the same sequence. A naive approach tries to fix this by making blocks bigger, but then simple patterns get lost in the averaging.

callout.html: Group repeating patterns into single tokens instead of chopping at fixed intervals.

steps.b: Scan the time series for common short patterns
steps.text: Extract all repeating motifs (e.g., flat, spike, ramp); rank by frequency.
Assign each top motif a unique ID: a compact lookup table matching patterns to codes.

steps.b: Replace matching stretches with motif tokens
steps.text: Wherever the data matches a motif, emit a single token instead of multiple samples.
The result is much shorter: flat parts merge, repetitions collapse, noise-like regions stay tokens.
Tweak token boundaries slightly after compression to maximize forecast accuracy, without retraining.

paras: The paper rewrites how a time series is converted into tokens. Instead of a rigid rule (every 10 samples becomes one token), it uses a learned motif vocabulary: patterns that actually appear in the data decide when to emit a token.

hidden.name: tokens per sample
paras: The hidden quantity is the efficiency of compression: how many tokens does the compressed sequence need, per original sample? Lower is better. This matters because the model's attention mechanism must store a table of all pairwise interactions between tokens; if you have 1000 tokens instead of 100, that table grows 100x, consuming memory and computation time.

The paper measures this by counting tokens before and after motif-based encoding, and also by tracking how much the final forecast error shrinks per unit of compression. A motif that compresses well but loses important detail is less useful than one that compresses less but preserves forecast quality.

heat.caption: Darker motifs compress better (appear more often). Light motifs are rare, so they add tokens selectively.

reads.html: A motif that appears in 40 percent of your data saves you 40 percent of your tokens if you use it, because every occurrence that would have been many separate tokens becomes a single motif token. The paper picks the motifs that save the most tokens while keeping forecast accuracy high, by ranking motifs by their compression value and discarding rare ones that add clutter.

The method greedily merges the most frequent samples into a discrete vocabulary of size K (tunable). Compression is exact: a sequence of N samples becomes N' tokens where N' ≤ N. The paper measures compression rate and forecast quality jointly.

paras: The core insight: a fixed chunking rule ignores the actual structure in the data. If you have a price that is flat for days, one token captures the whole thing. But fixed chunking assigns one token per hour, wasting nine. Pattern-based tokenization inverts this: find what the data naturally repeats, then use those repetitions as token boundaries.

Conditional decoding is the second part. After you compress using motifs, the token boundaries are locked in. But you can then tweak the reconstruction (how you turn tokens back into time series values) without retraining the model. This is a cheap optimization: it adjusts which exact value each motif token represents, so that the final forecast is more accurate. No gradient updates needed; just a direct calculation.

stages.s: Assign each pattern a motif ID
Replace matching stretches with motif tokens
Apply conditional decoding to polish token values

math.words: For each motif, store its average value and how many times it was chosen. During reconstruction, each token is replaced by its motif's average. Conditional decoding then solves for the per-motif value that minimizes forecast error, given the token sequence already fixed.
math.equation: reconstruction_value_m = mean of samples assigned to motif m; error = sum over time steps (predicted - true)^2; conditional_decoding shifts each motif's value by delta_m to minimize error without changing tokens
symbols: the numeric value assigned to motif m when decoding back to time series
a small adjustment per motif during conditional decoding
the sum of squared differences between forecast and real values
the compressed sequence using motif IDs instead of raw samples

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Motif A (flat): appears 400 times in the original 1000-sample series. Compressed to 1 token.
Motif B (spike): appears 200 times. Compressed to 1 token.
Motif C (rise): appears 300 times. Compressed to 1 token.
Motif D (noise, rare): appears 100 times. Stays as 100 tokens (too rare to compress).
Original: 1000 tokens. After motif encoding: 1 + 1 + 1 + 100 = 103 tokens. Compression ratio: 1000 / 103 = 9.7x.
Conditional decoding: instead of average value 45 for motif A, adjust to 46.2 if that shrinks forecast error. Same token count (103), but 48% lower error on validation data.

math.note: The fixed step-size tokenization would use 100 tokens per 100 samples; motifs reduce this to 1 per 100 repeated samples, saving computation proportional to pattern redundancy.

bars.h2: How much better does it get

charts.title: Naive fixed-chunk tokenization
charts.note: Baseline: every 10 samples make one token, regardless of content. Works everywhere but wastes tokens.

charts.title: This paper (motif-based + conditional decoding)
charts.note: Pattern-based tokenization saves 96% of tokens (25x compression). Forecast error drops 46%, and model prediction runs 8.4x faster because the model processes fewer tokens per pass.

items.html: If you pick only the top 2 motifs because they are so common, rare but important patterns such as a sudden shock in price disappear entirely. The compression is great, but forecast error rises because you erased critical structure.

If you scan one time series and build a motif vocabulary custom to it, those motifs may not appear in a different time series. Transfer to a new forecasting task will fail because the token vocabulary has no relevant patterns.

If you adjust motif values (delta_m) too aggressively without any constraint, the reconstruction can flip to unphysical values (e.g., negative prices). A lightweight regularization (penalizing large shifts) prevents this.

Calibrate motif vocabulary on a held-out training set, then apply it to a fresh time series. Conditional decoding uses a fixed learning rate small enough to stay stable. Test forecast error on a validation set separate from both. The compression persists across datasets if you pick motifs that are generalizable (e.g., flat, slow-rise, fast-drop) rather than data-specific.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Simulate a synthetic time series with 1000 samples: a flat region (50 samples), then a smooth rise (100 samples), then a spike (20 samples), then noise (830 samples). Train a simple regression model on the time series using a foundation model's (pretrained) encoder.

Measure: (1) token count before and after motif encoding, (2) validation forecast error before (using fixed tokens) and after (using motif tokens + conditional decoding), and (3) time to run the model on 10 new test sequences.
demo.metric_eq: compression_ratio = tokens_before / tokens_after; error_reduction = (error_fixed - error_motif) / error_fixed; speedup = time_fixed / time_motif
demo.closing: The demo must show all three: token count cut by 50 percent (motif tokens replace many samples with one token); error drops 20 percent (motif tokens align with real patterns, so the model sees real structure instead of arbitrary chunk boundaries); and prediction is 2x faster (fewer tokens means the attention table is smaller, so each forward pass takes half the time).
